text: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?
reference_answer: A list is mutable (elements can be changed after creation) and defined with square brackets. A tuple is immutable (cannot be changed after creation) and defined with parentheses. Tuples are generally faster and can be used as dictionary keys because they are hashable. Lists are preferred when the data needs to change; tuples when it should stay constant.

text: Explain how you would find the time complexity of an algorithm.
reference_answer: Time complexity describes how an algorithm's runtime scales with input size. To determine it: count the basic operations (comparisons, assignments) as a function of n; ignore constants; keep the dominant term. A single loop is O(n), nested loops over n are O(n²), halving the input each step is O(log n). Always identify best, worst, and average cases where they differ.

text: What is Object-Oriented Programming and what are its four main principles?
reference_answer: OOP organises code around objects that combine data (attributes) and behaviour (methods). The four principles are: Encapsulation — bundling data and methods and hiding internal details; Inheritance — a class deriving properties from a parent class; Polymorphism — different classes sharing the same interface; Abstraction — exposing only essential details.

text: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue, and give a use case for each.
reference_answer: A stack follows LIFO (Last In, First Out): the last element pushed is the first popped. Use cases include function call stacks and undo operations. A queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out): the first element enqueued is the first dequeued. Use cases include print spoolers, BFS traversal, and task scheduling.

text: What is the difference between == and is in Python?
reference_answer: == compares values (are the contents equal?). is compares identity (are they the exact same object in memory?). For example, two lists with the same elements are == but not is. Always use is when checking against None (e.g. if x is None) because None is a singleton.

text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
reference_answer: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregate functions have been applied. Example: WHERE age > 18 filters rows before grouping; HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 filters groups with more than five members.

text: Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN.
reference_answer: INNER JOIN returns only rows where there is a match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right; where there is no match, right-side columns are NULL. Use INNER JOIN when you only care about matches; LEFT JOIN when you need all records from the left table regardless.

text: What is the difference between a mean and a median?
reference_answer: The mean is the arithmetic average (sum divided by count). The median is the middle value when data is sorted. The median is more robust to outliers — for example, in salary data with a few very high earners, the median better represents the typical salary. Use mean when the distribution is roughly symmetric; median when it is skewed or has outliers.

text: What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript?
reference_answer: var is function-scoped and hoisted (initialised to undefined). let and const are block-scoped and not initialised at hoisting (temporal dead zone). let allows reassignment; const does not (though object properties can still change). In modern code, prefer const by default and let when reassignment is needed; avoid var.

They solve the difficulty of reusing stateful logic across components and make code easier to understand. Key hooks include useState (local state), useEffect (side effects, replaces lifecycle methods), useContext, useRef, and useMemo.

text: What is a REST API and what are its main principles?
reference_answer: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked APIs using standard HTTP methods. Key principles: stateless (no session state on the server), resources identified by URLs, standard HTTP verbs (GET to read, POST to create, PUT/PATCH to update, DELETE to remove), responses typically in JSON, and uniform interface. Idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) return the same result when called multiple times.

text: Explain the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases.
reference_answer: SQL (relational) databases use tables with fixed schemas, support complex queries and joins, and follow ACID properties. NoSQL databases (document, key-value, column, graph) have flexible schemas and are designed for scalability and specific data models. SQL suits structured data with complex relationships (finance, ERP). NoSQL suits unstructured or rapidly evolving data at scale (real-time apps, content).

text: What is a process and how is it different from a thread?
reference_answer: A process is an independent program in execution with its own memory space (address space, heap, stack). A thread is a unit of execution within a process; threads share the process's memory and resources. Creating a thread is cheaper than a new process (lighter context switch). Processes are isolated (a crash in one doesn't affect others), while threads in the same process can corrupt shared memory.

text: Explain how Dijkstra's algorithm works and its time complexity when implemented with a min-priority queue.
reference_answer: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source node to all other nodes in a graph with non-negative edge weights. It maintains tentative distances, initialized to infinity except 0 for the source. Using a min-priority queue (min-heap), it repeatedly extracts the node with the smallest distance, visits each neighbor, and performs edge relaxation (updating distances if a shorter path is found). Its time complexity with an adjacency list and binary min-heap is O((V + E) log V). It does not work reliably with negative edge weights.

text: What are the core architectural principles of RESTful API design?
reference_answer: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style based on: 1) Client-server separation; 2) Statelessness (each request contains all needed information); 3) Uniform interface with URI-identified resources (nouns) and HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE); 4) Explicit caching controls via HTTP headers; 5) Layered system architecture. Key principles include proper use of status codes (200, 201, 400, 404, 500) and adhering to idempotency for GET, PUT, and DELETE.

text: Explain database normalization and the difference between Second Normal Form (2NF) and Third Normal Form (3NF).
reference_answer: Normalization organizes database relations to reduce data redundancy and eliminate insert, update, and delete anomalies. 1NF requires atomic values and unique records. 2NF requires 1NF plus eliminating partial dependencies (every non-key attribute must depend on the whole composite primary key). 3NF requires 2NF plus eliminating transitive dependencies (non-key attributes must depend directly on the primary key, not through another non-key attribute: 'nothing but the key').

text: Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous programming, and how event loops manage concurrency.
reference_answer: In synchronous programming, operations execute sequentially and block the thread until completion. In asynchronous programming, long-running operations (like network requests or file I/O) are dispatched without blocking the execution thread, allowing other tasks to proceed. The runtime uses an event loop, call stack, and task queue to process completed asynchronous callbacks when the stack clears. In modern languages, promises and async/await syntax provide clean asynchronous control flow.

text: How would you design a distributed rate limiter to handle millions of requests across multiple servers?
reference_answer: A distributed rate limiter throttles incoming requests per user, IP, or API key. Common algorithms include Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counter. In a distributed environment, rate limits are stored in a centralized, low-latency in-memory cache such as Redis. Using Redis Lua scripts or atomic increments ensures atomicity and avoids race conditions across multiple application nodes. When the limit is reached, return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. For resilience, fall back to local in-memory limiting if Redis is temporarily unreachable.

text: What is a race condition in concurrent software, and how do mutexes, semaphores, and deadlocks relate to it?
reference_answer: A race condition occurs when multiple threads concurrently access and modify shared memory, causing non-deterministic outcomes depending on execution order. To prevent this, critical sections must be synchronized. A mutex (mutual exclusion) allows only one thread to access a resource at a time. A semaphore is a signaling mechanism maintaining a counter, allowing up to N threads access. Deadlock happens when two or more threads are permanently blocked waiting for locks held by each other, typically satisfying Coffman's conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

text: What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript, and what is variable hoisting?
reference_answer: var is function-scoped and hoisted to the top of its scope initialized as undefined, which often led to subtle bugs. let and const are block-scoped (scoped to curly braces {}) introduced in ES6. While let and const are also hoisted, they remain in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) and throw a ReferenceError if accessed before declaration. const variables cannot be reassigned, whereas let variables can. However, objects declared with const can still have their internal properties mutated.

text: Explain event bubbling, event capturing, and event delegation in the browser DOM.
reference_answer: DOM event propagation has three phases: capturing (event travels down from window to target), target phase, and bubbling (event bubbles up from target back to window). Event delegation leverages bubbling by attaching a single event listener to a common parent element rather than individual child elements. The handler inspects event.target to determine which child triggered the action, reducing memory overhead and automatically handling dynamically added elements.

text: What are React Hooks, why were they introduced, and what rules must you follow when using them?
reference_answer: React Hooks allow functional components to use state, lifecycle events, and side effects without writing class components. They were introduced to promote logic reuse through custom hooks, simplify complex component code, and eliminate 'this' binding pitfalls. The two essential Rules of Hooks are: 1) Only call hooks at the top level (never inside loops, conditions, or nested functions); 2) Only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks. This ensures React maintains hook state across renders using call order.

text: How does the Virtual DOM work in React, and how does reconciliation optimize rendering performance?
reference_answer: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory JavaScript representation of the real DOM. When state or props change, React generates a new Virtual DOM tree and runs a diffing algorithm (reconciliation) comparing it with the previous snapshot. React calculates the minimum set of mutations and batches updates to the real DOM. React optimizes this to O(n) complexity using heuristics: elements of different types generate different trees, and the 'key' prop enables tracking list items across renders without re-mounting.

text: What is a closure in JavaScript, and what is a practical real-world scenario where you would use one?

An inner function retains access to variables declared in its outer function's scope even after the outer function has finished executing. Practical applications include: 1) Data encapsulation and private state (e.g., creating module patterns with private variables); 2) Function factories and currying; 3) Debounce or throttle utility functions where timer state is preserved across repeated invocations.

text: Explain the differences between CSS Flexbox and CSS Grid, and provide guidelines on when to choose one over the other.
reference_answer: Flexbox is one-dimensional: it handles layout along a single axis (either row or column) at a time, making it ideal for aligning UI components, navigation bars, button groups, and linear content flows. CSS Grid is two-dimensional: it simultaneously manages both rows and columns, making it suited for overall page layout, complex dashboard grids, and card galleries with fixed aspect ratios. A common pattern is using Grid for the macroeconomic page skeleton and Flexbox for micro-alignments inside components.

text: How do you evaluate and structure state management in a large-scale frontend application?
reference_answer: In large frontend applications, state should be categorized into four distinct layers: 1) Local UI state (useState/useReducer) for component-specific interactions like modal visibility; 2) Server state (TanStack Query/RTK Query) for asynchronous backend data with automatic caching, background refetching, and deduping; 3) URL state (search params) for shareable filter/pagination state; 4) Global client state (Zustand/Redux) reserved strictly for app-wide user preferences, cart, or authenticated sessions. text: What is the difference between HTTP GET, POST, PUT, and PATCH methods, and what does idempotency mean?
reference_answer: GET retrieves a resource; it is safe and idempotent (produces no side effects). POST creates a subordinate resource; it is neither safe nor idempotent (calling it multiple times creates multiple records). PUT replaces the entire target resource with the uploaded payload; it is idempotent because multiple identical PUT requests leave the server in the same state. PATCH applies partial modifications to an existing resource and is generally non-idempotent by default. Idempotency means multiple identical requests have the same intended effect as a single request.

text: How do database indexes work under the hood, and what are the trade-offs of adding multiple indexes to a table?
reference_answer: Most relational database indexes use B-Tree or B+ Tree data structures. A B+ Tree keeps data sorted with high fan-out, storing keys in internal nodes and all actual row pointers/data in leaf nodes linked sequentially. This reduces disk I/O to O(log N) for point lookups and range scans. Trade-offs: while indexes dramatically accelerate read queries, every insert, update, and delete must update the index structures, adding write latency and consuming additional memory and disk space. High cardinality columns benefit most from indexing.

text: Explain the architectural trade-offs between a monolithic system and a microservices architecture.
reference_answer: A monolith bundles all business logic, data models, and deployables in a single codebase. Benefits include simple local development, straightforward ACID transactions, easy debugging, and zero inter-service network latency. Downsides include shared blast radius, scaling limits, and deployment bottlenecks in large teams. Microservices divide functionality into loosely coupled, independently deployable services around business domains. Benefits are independent scalability and tech stack flexibility. Drawbacks include distributed complexity, network overhead, eventual consistency challenges, and heavy DevOps/monitoring requirements.

text: How do you maintain data consistency across distributed services without distributed two-phase commit locks?
reference_answer: In distributed microservices, traditional Two-Phase Commit (2PC) creates blocking locks and single points of failure. Instead, systems use eventual consistency and the Saga Pattern: a sequence of local transactions where each service updates its own database and publishes an event or message. If a step fails, the saga executes compensating transactions in reverse order to undo earlier actions. Sagas can be implemented via Choreography (event-driven) or Orchestration (central coordinator). The Transactional Outbox pattern guarantees reliable event publishing without dual-write failures.

text: What are SQL Injection, XSS, and CSRF vulnerabilities, and what concrete measures prevent them?
reference_answer: SQL Injection occurs when untrusted user input alters database SQL commands; prevent it by using parameterized queries (prepared statements) or ORMs, never concatenating raw strings. XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects malicious client-side scripts into web pages; prevent it with output encoding, strict Content Security Policy (CSP), and avoiding unsafe innerHTML. CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks authenticated users into submitting unwanted requests; prevent it using anti-CSRF synchronizer tokens and configuring cookies with SameSite=Strict/Lax and HttpOnly flags.

text: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and how do JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) work?
reference_answer: Authentication verifies identity ('who you are'), e.g. through passwords or MFA. Authorization verifies permissions ('what you are allowed to do'), e.g. role-based access control. A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe token containing three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots: Header (algorithm), Payload (claims like user_id and expiration exp), and Signature (header and payload hashed with a secret key or signed with a private key). Because servers verify the signature without querying a central session database, JWTs enable stateless authentication.

text: Explain the CAP theorem and how it guides architectural trade-offs in distributed database selection.
reference_answer: The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every non-failing node returns a non-error response), and Partition Tolerance (the system functions despite arbitrary network message loss). Because network partitions are inevitable in real-world distributed networks, systems must choose between Consistency (CP, like HBase, CockroachDB, preferring errors over stale data) and Availability (AP, like Cassandra, DynamoDB, returning potentially stale data with eventual consistency).

text: Describe common caching strategies (Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Back) and how you handle cache invalidation.
reference_answer: In Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading), the application checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads from the DB, stores the result in cache, and returns it. In Write-Through, the application writes to the cache and DB simultaneously, keeping data fresh at the cost of higher write latency. In Write-Back (Write-Behind), data is written only to cache and asynchronously flushed to the database, maximizing write performance but risking data loss if the cache crashes. Invalidation strategies rely on TTL (Time-To-Live), explicit deletion on updates, and mutex locks to prevent cache stampedes.

text: Explain SQL window functions and contrast ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK with a concrete use case.
reference_answer: Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows related to the current row without collapsing them into a single row like GROUP BY. With PARTITION BY and ORDER BY: ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique sequential integer to each row, breaking ties arbitrarily (1, 2, 3, 4). RANK() assigns identical ranks to ties and skips subsequent numbers (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK() assigns identical ranks to ties without skipping numbers (1, 2, 2, 3). A typical use case is finding the top 3 highest-earning employees per department.

text: How would you explain A/B testing, statistical significance, and p-values to a non-technical marketing stakeholder?
reference_answer: Explain by analogy: an A/B test is like comparing two coin designs to see which lands heads more often. We randomly split users into Group A (current version) and Group B (new version). Because random noise always exists, statistical significance tells us whether the difference in conversion rate is real or just luck. A p-value is the probability that we would see this improvement purely by random coincidence if the change actually had zero effect. If the p-value is under 5% (p < 0.05), we can be 95% confident the new design genuinely caused the uplift.

text: If daily active users (DAU) dropped suddenly by 15% overnight, how would you systematically investigate the root cause?

text: What is the difference between a star schema and a snowflake schema in data warehousing?
reference_answer: Both are dimensional modeling techniques for data warehouses centered around fact tables containing numeric metrics. In a Star Schema, dimension tables are completely denormalized, meaning each dimension is represented by a single table directly joined to the fact table. This yields simpler SQL queries, fewer joins, and faster read performance for BI tools. In a Snowflake Schema, dimension tables are normalized into sub-dimension tables (e.g. splitting product into product, category, and brand), reducing storage redundancy but requiring more complex multi-table joins.

text: What are Type I and Type II errors in hypothesis testing, and what are the practical implications of each in business?
reference_answer: A Type I error is a False Positive (rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true; alpha level, typically 5%). In business, this means concluding a new website feature works when it doesn't, wasting engineering resources. A Type II error is a False Negative (failing to reject the null hypothesis when an effect actually exists; beta level, related to statistical power 1 - beta). In business, this means discarding an effective feature because the sample size was too small to detect the difference. Balancing them depends on the cost of false optimism versus missed opportunities.

text: How do you define success metrics and establish a North Star Metric for a new product feature?

text: Walk me through how you conduct user discovery interviews to uncover unarticulated customer pain points.

text: If a well-funded competitor launches a feature copying your product at a lower price point, how do you respond?

text: What is a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), and how do you decide what belongs in Version 1.0 versus future releases?
reference_answer: An MVP is the smallest version of a new product or feature that allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort. It is not an unfinished product, but rather a functional end-to-end slice delivering core value (the 'skateboard' in the skateboard-to-car metaphor). To scope v1.0: identify the central hypothesis being tested; include only features indispensable to solving the single primary pain point; defer secondary enhancements, advanced configuration, and automated edge cases to fast-follow iterations guided by actual usage data.
